title: 'Learn to Code' Is Dead: Andrew Yang Says AI Will Devour Half of Entry-Level White-Collar Jobs
excerpt: The former presidential candidate warns that autonomous coding tools are gutting tech hiring — a jolt for hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin engineers and STEM graduates in the US
body:
Andrew Yang built a presidential campaign on a simple thesis: automation is coming for American jobs, and nobody in Washington is paying attention. Six years later, the former Democratic candidate says the reality has outrun even his own dire predictions.

"I just came from an AI conference out West," Yang said in a recent television appearance that has since ricocheted across tech forums and South Asian professional networks. "They said to me that what we're going to see in the next six months outstrips what we've seen in the last 10 years because the rate of change is on a hockey stick and heading up."

## The Company That Grew 100-Fold

Yang pointed to one company developing autonomous coding systems whose revenue had increased "100-fold in the last 12 months" — a figure that, if accurate, signals an extraordinary pace of corporate adoption. The implication is blunt: software development tasks once performed by junior engineers are being absorbed by AI tools at a speed that hiring pipelines cannot accommodate.

"If that continues, it's going to eat a lot of the tech budgets from major corporates that used to go to humans," Yang said. "And so you're seeing the employment of recent computer science graduates fall off a cliff from a lot of programs."

The timing is painfully ironic. Just four years ago, the universal career advice for young people was to learn to code. "And now the opposite of that is true," Yang said flatly.

## Dario Amodei's 50 Percent Warning

Yang also cited Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has publicly estimated that AI could automate up to 50 percent of entry-level white-collar jobs within the next several years. "I believe him," Yang said. The warning extends well beyond software engineering into finance, legal research, marketing and customer service — sectors that collectively employ millions of degree-holding workers.

Yang described the mechanism in blunt terms: "The easiest people to fire are the people you haven't hired yet." He pointed to data suggesting that underemployment among recent college graduates has climbed above 50 percent, and that unemployment rates for degree holders are approaching those of workers without college credentials.

## Why This Hits the Diaspora Hardest

For Indian-American and South Asian families in the United States, Yang's warnings carry a particular sting. The community has long treated STEM careers — particularly computer science and engineering — as the surest pathway to economic stability. Indian-origin workers make up a disproportionate share of the US tech workforce, with hundreds of thousands employed on H-1B visas tied directly to their employers.

The arithmetic is stark. Meta announced this week that it will cut thousands of managers and reassign 7,000 employees into AI-focused roles. LinkedIn is trimming staff across multiple departments. Walmart is relocating 1,000 corporate employees in a tech restructuring. Each of these moves affects the Indian-origin workforce disproportionately, given its heavy concentration in US technology roles.

For H-1B holders, a layoff does not simply mean unemployment — it triggers a 60-day clock to find a new sponsor or leave the country. When hiring freezes compound with AI-driven role elimination, the visa system transforms from a gateway into a trap.

## No Consensus on the End Game

Economists and labour experts remain divided on whether AI will ultimately destroy more jobs than it creates. Some analysts argue that previous waves of automation — from the loom to the spreadsheet — displaced workers in the short term but generated entirely new categories of employment. Others counter that generative AI is qualitatively different: it targets cognitive work, the very domain where educated workers were supposed to be safe.

Yang's prescription has been consistent since 2019: universal basic income, retraining programmes and a fundamental rethinking of how Americans prepare for careers. Whether Washington listens remains an open question. What is no longer debatable is the speed at which the ground is shifting beneath the feet of a generation that was told coding was the answer.
